newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Errant MP puts NZ government majority at risk.
newsitem.headline: Errant MP puts NZ government majority at risk.

text.p: The centre-right New Zealand government's one seat majority was in the balance on Friday as Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters considered the future of an MP who admitted offering to sell his story to the media.

Peters said he had yet to decide what to do with MP Tukoroirangi Morgan after he admitted on Thursday trying to sell an exclusive television interview for NZ$20,000 (nearly $14,000) to help fund two libel actions he is involved in.

Morgan, a Maori MP from the junior coalition partner New Zealand First led by Peters, at first denied knowledge of the attempt to Peters, prompting the party leader to issue a statement of support which he later had to retract.

Amid widespread calls for Morgan to be forced to resign, including editorials in all three major national morning newspapers on Friday, Peters said he would consider his next move in consultation with his colleagues.

"I have spoken to (Morgan) on the basis of what actually did happen. I have yet to complete discussions on that. Whilst some people would want to rush to judgment, that is not in the nature of things as far as this party is concerned," he told reporters.
One political source told Reuters that Peters was likely to make his decision known before parliament next sits on Tuesday.
The formal coalition combination of the conservative National Party and New Zealand First holds 61-seats in Wellington's 120-seat single chamber.
Based on the results of recent opinion polls, a by-election in Morgan's Te Tai Hauauru seat would likely be won by the largest opposition party, Labour.
But even if the government lost the seat, it would be unlikely to fall or see its programme under threat.
It can rely on stated positions of support from eight MPs from free-market party Act and the lone centrist United Party MP Peter Dunne on matters of confidence and revenue raising.
Dunne said he remained prepared to support the government, but it was too early to discuss details of cooperation.
"I am not going to be treated as the next sub off the bench," he told Reuters.
"I am supporting them on confidence now. The coalition agreement provides for the entrance of new parties by negotiation.
"I think the government will prefer to deal with me (than with Act)," Dunne said.
When he finally gave a television interview on Thursday night -- for which he was not paid -- Morgan said he knew his political future lay in Peters' hands.
"I joined a party which advocated and promoted accountability. I wait for a response from my leader. And at the end of the day, it's his decision," he said.
Peters made clear earlier in the day that this was Morgan's last chance, saying "any such repetition of a mistake of this nature in future will lead to very severe consequences".
Opposition MPs have called for Morgan to go, although Labour leader Helen Clark said in a radio interview she expected the government would try to ride out the storm.
By sacking Morgan, New Zealand First might risk losing his brother-in-law, Maori Affairs Minister Tau Henare, and at least two other MPs to a breakaway Maori party, Clark said.

Morgan has been a recurring source of embarrassment for the government since the October 1996 election with revelations about spending of funds from a cash-strapped pilot Maori language television channel ATN where he used to work.
A Serious Fraud Office inquiry into the financial affairs of the channel is nearing completion and widely expected to be released next week.
